title: Proofs and reasons: How math works in the mind
gist: Santa Fe Institute's Oct 2026 working group on the cognitive science of mathematical proof is motivated by AI moving from textbook theorems to frontier proofs in about three years, raising the question of whether humans can understand machine mathematics.

insights.claim: Simon DeDeo says AI went from proving undergraduate-textbook theorems about three years ago to proving theorems once considered at the outer edge of human possibility.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Evidence that AI reasoning capability in formal mathematics is advancing very fast; track math benchmarks as a capability proxy.
insights.quote: Three years ago, machines were proving theorems in undergraduate textbooks
insights.locator: The working group comes at a watershed moment

insights.claim: The article frames the present as a watershed moment for mathematics because machine-generated proofs now reach the frontier of human capability.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Signals that automated discovery is becoming credible in pure research domains, not only applied ones.
insights.locator: The working group comes at a watershed moment

insights.claim: Once a proof exists, human or machine, other mathematicians must work to understand it, and it is unclear how AI-produced mathematics will overlap with human cognition.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: A bottleneck may shift from finding proofs to verifying and interpreting them, which affects the value of human oversight in AI-driven research.
insights.locator: Once a proof has been solved

insights.claim: Researchers want to know how AI systems approach hard problems and how far their results will be accessible to humans.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Interpretability of AI reasoning is an open research question; watch for work on legibility of AI outputs.
insights.locator: As AI systems tackle increasingly advanced problems

insights.claim: Mathematics, art and theological thinking confer no apparent evolutionary advantage, demand extreme concentration and stretch human mental limits, but only mathematics can be compared across cultures and eras on equal footing.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Mathematics is positioned as a clean testbed for the limits of the mind, useful for benchmarking human versus machine reasoning.

insights.claim: Despite proof dating back at least to Euclid around 300 BCE, little is known about what happens in the mind when humans solve proofs.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Highlights a long-standing research gap that new AI results make more pressing.
insights.locator: Mathematical proof dates back at least to Euclid

insights.claim: The Santa Fe Institute working group 'Proofs and Reasons: Toward a Cognitive Science of Real Mathematics' met Oct. 13-15, 2026, bringing together mathematicians, cognitive scientists, computer scientists and philosophers.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Marks early institutional formation of a research field at the AI-math-cognition intersection.

insights.claim: DeDeo says this is the first of three planned meetings aimed at a special issue of papers, and that the group is positioned to kick off a new area of scientific research.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Expect follow-on meetings and a special issue; a possible source of future research outputs on AI and mathematical understanding.
insights.quote: We think we’re in a position to kick off a new area of scientific research
insights.locator: DeDeo says these themes include many open questions

insights.claim: The meeting was funded in part by Grant 63750, 'Explaining Universal', from the John Templeton Foundation.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Shows philanthropic funding is backing foundational work on AI and human reasoning.
insights.locator: This meeting was funded in part
